mcqs.question: What makes scope creep on a take-home particularly dangerous compared to other mistakes?
options: It feels productive the entire time it's happening, making it invisible until you check the clock
It's usually caused by a single deliberate decision that's easy to catch and reverse
It only affects the README, not the actual code quality
It's exclusively a problem for advanced-level take-homes, not beginner ones
mcqs.explanation: Scope creep is dangerous precisely because each small addition feels like reasonable progress in the moment, so there's no natural signal to stop until time has already been lost. It's rarely one deliberate decision, it affects code and time budget directly, and it isn't limited to any particular difficulty level.

mcqs.question: A take-home suggests 4 hours; you end up spending 15 and submit without mentioning it. What's the problem with this?
options: It's fine as long as the final code quality is high
It misrepresents your actual working speed, since evaluators calibrate their read against the reported time
It's only a problem if the extra time was spent on features outside scope
There's no issue since take-homes don't actually track time spent
mcqs.explanation: Evaluators read a submission's quality relative to the time reportedly spent — an undisclosed 15-hour effort presented as a 4-hour one misrepresents your actual pace, regardless of whether the extra time went to in-scope or out-of-scope work. Time reporting matters independently of code quality.

mcqs.question: What is the recommended way to triage an ambiguous requirement in an async take-home?
options: Always ask a clarifying question regardless of how minor the ambiguity is
Never ask, since asking questions signals you can't work independently
Build two full versions of the feature to cover both interpretations
Assess whether the ambiguity is architecture-changing: ask if it is, document an assumption if it's minor
mcqs.explanation: Triage means matching the response to the stakes — a genuinely architecture-changing ambiguity warrants a specific question, while a minor one is fine to resolve with a documented assumption. Asking about everything or nothing are both worse defaults, and building duplicate versions wastes the time budget entirely.

mcqs.question: Why is submitting a take-home with zero tests risky, even for a small exercise?
options: Automated grading scripts always fail submissions with no test files
Tests are the only part of a submission an evaluator actually reads
Many rubrics score testing discipline directly, and zero tests reads as an oversight or a belief testing doesn't matter
It's risky only if the take-home explicitly mentions writing tests
mcqs.explanation: Testing discipline is frequently scored as its own signal, independent of an explicit instruction to write tests — skipping it entirely sends an unintended message about priorities. It isn't the only thing evaluators read, and grading scripts don't universally require test files to pass.

mcqs.question: Why is a deliberate pre-submission checklist recommended instead of trusting your own sense that things are fine?
options: Because evaluators require a checklist to be included as a literal file
Because each pitfall it catches feels invisible or reasonable from the inside while you're mid-task
Because checklists are only useful for junior candidates, not experienced ones
Because it replaces the need to write a trade-offs section
mcqs.explanation: Scope creep, silent guessing, and skipped tests all feel like reasonable behavior in the moment — that's exactly why an explicit final check catches what momentum and self-assessment miss. It isn't a literal deliverable requirement, it applies at any experience level, and it complements rather than replaces the trade-offs section.
